strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap: Merlin-Arthur Classifiers (PVGs) have not been demonstrated on high-dimensional inputs, and CBMs are limited by linear heads. NCV is a natural and sensible bridge between these two research lines, and the framework is clearly motivated and easy to follow.

The experimental scope is broad and mostly convincing: four datasets spanning synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) to large-scale real-world data (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k), evaluation over 10-20 random seeds with standard deviations, and useful ablations (mask sizes, Set Transformer vs. MLP feature selectors, alternative architectures in Tables 4-9).

Two concept-extractor instantiations (supervised-free NCB and CLIP-based) support the claim of generality of the framework, and the shortcut-mitigation study with varying clean-data ratios (Tables 2 and 6) is a thoughtful addition that goes beyond the core design claim.

The limitations section is honest and substantive, explicitly acknowledging dependence on concept extractor quality, training instability of the three-agent game, and inherited CLIP biases, which is appropriate treatment of limitations.
Supplementary materials provide enough detail (architectures, hyperparameters, seeds, epochs, learning rates) for reasonable reproducibility.
weaknesses: The reported 'pretraining' results (Table 7) appear to undermine a central claim: the verifier pretrained without provers achieves 85.96% on CIFAR-100 and 77.07% on ImageNet-1k, yet final NCV completeness is only 83.32% and 67.04%. The PVG training thus substantially *reduces* accuracy over a simple nonlinear classifier on the same concepts on real-world data, but this discrepancy is never analyzed or even mentioned, weakening the Q2 claim of narrowing the interpretability-accuracy gap.

The perfect soundness results (100.00±0.00 across 20 seeds on CLEVR-Hans) raise the concern that soundness may be trivially achievable: since the verifier has a rejection class and soundness is defined as 'correct class or rejection', a degenerate verifier could attain perfect soundness by always rejecting under adversarially selected concepts. No rejection rates are reported anywhere, so the soundness metric's meaningfulness cannot be assessed.

Novelty is fairly incremental: the method is essentially the existing MAC setup applied to frozen concept encodings from existing extractors (NCB, CLIP/SpLiCE), with standard Set Transformer/MLP agents. The formal guarantees of Wäldchen et al. (2024) are acknowledged to not extend to multi-class settings, so 'verifiable' and 'certifiable' claims are weaker than the framing suggests; empirical results carry most of the weight.

Baseline fairness and completeness are questionable: Pixel-MAC scores only 15.27% on CIFAR-100, suggesting the pixel-space baseline may be undertuned; the main Table 1 omits a nonlinear CBM (MLP on concepts) baseline, which is the most direct competitor for 'nonlinear head on concepts' and appears only in the shortcut study where the margin over it is modest.

The claim of more detailed, human-understandable explanations (Q3) is supported only by qualitative figures on synthetic CLEVR data; no user study or quantitative interpretability metric is provided, and the discussion itself concedes CLIP-based concept spaces may diverge from human semantics.

Presentation/citation hygiene issues: placeholder arXiv identifiers (e.g., 'arXiv:2401.xxxxx', 'arXiv:2106.xxxxx'), duplicated Set Transformer references (2019a/2019b), and inconsistent citation style reduce polish and reproducibility.

The claim that NCV 'surpasses ResNet-18 on natural images' (Q1/Q2) is a small margin on ImageNet (67.04 vs. 66.16) against a relatively weak backbone (ResNet-18), so the headline claim of matching opaque SOTA-style models is overstated relative to the evidence.

strengths: The core idea of shifting the Merlin-Arthur prover-verifier interaction from pixel space to concept encodings is sensible and addresses a real scalability limitation of PVGs on high-dimensional images.
Experiments cover synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) and real-world (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k) benchmarks, with multiple random seeds (20/10) and standard deviations reported.
The paper includes useful ablations: mask sizes, feature-selector architectures (Tables 4, 5, 8, 9), and shortcut experiments with varying ratios of clean data (Tables 2, 6).

The paper is generally well written and organized around clear research questions (Q1-Q4), with an honest limitations discussion covering dependence on concept extractor quality, training instability, and inherited CLIP biases.
Two concept extractor instantiations (NCB and CLIP-based) demonstrate some generality of the framework.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: NCV is essentially a straightforward composition of existing components (the Merlin-Arthur Classifier of Wäldchen et al. 2024 applied on top of existing concept extractors such as NCB and CLIP/SpLiCE), with no new theory or algorithmic contribution. The paper acknowledges that the information-theoretic guarantees of MAC do not carry over to the multi-class, high-dimensional setting considered here.

The paper's own supplementary material undermines the central accuracy claims. Table 7 shows that the pretrained verifier without provers achieves 85.96% on CIFAR-100 and 77.07% on ImageNet-1k, which is substantially higher than the final NCV results reported in Table 1 (83.32% and 67.04%). Thus, on real-world data, the full NCV pipeline actually degrades accuracy relative to a plain nonlinear classifier on the same concept features, contradicting the claim that NCV 'narrows the interpretability-accuracy gap'. Table 1 omits this pretrained-verifier baseline.

Similarly, on CLEVR the pretraining results (Table 3: 98.13/97.83 test accuracy) are close to the final NCV results (98.92/97.89), suggesting that most of the improvement over linear CBMs comes from the nonlinear verifier rather than from the prover-verifier game itself. A nonlinear-CBM baseline is only included in the shortcut experiments (Tables 2 and 6), not in the main comparison (Table 1), so the specific benefit of the PVG objective is not isolated in Q1/Q2.
The claimed shortcut robustness is mixed: in Table 6 (CLEVR-Hans3), at 0% clean data NCV has a larger validation-test gap (5.23) than the nonlinear CBM (3.66), which is glossed over in the main text.

Soundness scores of ~100% (often 100.00±0.00) across all methods including Pixel-MAC raise questions about the discriminative power and calibration of the soundness metric; no soundness-under-distribution-shift or stronger adversarial evaluation is provided.

Explanation quality (Q3) is supported only by qualitative examples on a synthetic dataset; no human study or quantitative faithfulness metric is offered, and the paper itself concedes object-level explanations are not available with the CLIP-based extractor.

Reproducibility is only partial: implementation details are given, but no code release or seeds/hyperparameter search protocol for the multi-agent training is described, and the min-max training is acknowledged to be potentially unstable.

Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: placeholder citations remain in the references (arXiv:2401.xxxxx, arXiv:2106.xxxxx), the Lee et al. Set Transformer reference is duplicated (2019a/2019b), and there are typographical errors (e.g., 'adverserial', 'inparticular').

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and genuinely novel in its combination: moving the Merlin-Arthur prover-verifier interaction from pixel space to concept encodings simultaneously addresses PVG scalability and the linear-classifier expressivity ceiling of CBMs.

The evaluation is broad, covering synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) and real-world benchmarks (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k), with multiple random seeds (20 for CLEVR-Hans, 10 for real-world) and reported standard deviations.
The framework is demonstrated with two distinct concept extractors (CLIP-based and unsupervised NCB), which supports the generality claim of the method rather than tying results to a single pipeline.
Ablation studies on mask sizes and prover architectures (Tables 4, 5, 8, 9) and a dedicated shortcut-mitigation study (Tables 2, 6) go beyond a single headline table.

The limitations section is honest and substantive, acknowledging dependence on concept extractor quality, training instability of the three-agent game, inherited CLIP biases, and the fact that formal information-theoretic guarantees do not yet extend to this multi-class nonlinear setting.
weaknesses: The paper's framing of accuracy results is potentially misleading. Supplementary Table 7 shows the pretrained verifier (without provers) achieves 85.96% on CIFAR-100 and 77.07% on ImageNet-1k, but NCV's final results are 83.32% and 67.04% — i.e., the PVG training actually degrades accuracy relative to its own initialization on both real-world datasets. The main text claims NCV 'surpasses ResNet-18 even in raw accuracy' without disclosing this regression, and no analysis of why PVG training hurts performance is provided.

The soundness metric may be trivially inflated by the rejection class. Since Arthur can abstain when given Morgana's concepts, near-100% soundness (100.00±0.00 on CLEVR-Hans) could be achieved simply by rejecting adversarial inputs. No rejection rates are reported for Merlin-selected vs. Morgana-selected inputs, so it is impossible to distinguish genuine robustness from a rejection-heavy policy that could also degrade completeness. This is a central evidential gap for the 'verifiable' claim.

A key baseline is missing from the main comparison: a nonlinear classifier (e.g., MLP) directly on concept encodings. This baseline appears only in the shortcut study (Table 2, 'CBM (nonlin.)') where it comes close to NCV, yet is absent from Table 1. Without it, the claimed benefit of the full three-agent PVG machinery over simply using a nonlinear head on concepts is not established.

The 'verifiability' language is stronger than what is shown. Wäldchen et al.'s information-theoretic guarantees cover binary classification under specific assumptions; the paper provides only empirical soundness against a jointly trained Morgana, and the formal guarantee gap is deferred to the conclusion rather than treated as a limitation of the central claim.

The explanation-quality claim (Q3) rests entirely on qualitative examples with no human evaluation or quantitative faithfulness metrics, despite human-understandability being a core motivation (Figure 1).

Signs of training instability are visible but undiscussed: Table 8 shows validation completeness of 71.20±22.43 for mask size 8 on CIFAR-100, an enormous variance that contradicts the paper's claim of improved min-max stability.

Reference hygiene is poor for a main-track submission: several citations contain placeholder arXiv numbers ('arXiv:2401.xxxxx', 'arXiv:2106.xxxxx') and 'and et al.' as author lists, and the Set Transformer reference is duplicated (Lee et al. 2019a/2019b).

The shortcut mitigation result is modest: the non-linear CBM baseline achieves comparable gaps (e.g., 3.66 vs. NCV's 5.23 at 0% clean data in Table 6, where NCV is actually worse), so the general claim of intrinsic shortcut robustness is only partially supported.

strengths: Clear and sensible core idea: shifting the Merlin-Arthur prover-verifier interaction from pixel space to a frozen, interpretable concept space, which directly addresses the known scalability and interpretability limitations of PVGs while relaxing the linear-classifier constraint of CBMs.

Broad and multi-seed empirical evaluation spanning synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) and real-world benchmarks (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, COCOLogic) with 10-20 random seeds, standard deviations, and meaningful baselines (ResNet, Pixel-MAC, linear/nonlinear CBMs, DCR).

Thorough ablations: mask size, gamma weighting (showing soundness collapses without the adversarial prover), prover architecture (Set Transformer vs MLP), and a computational cost comparison showing NCV is 1-3 orders of magnitude cheaper than Pixel-MAC.

The shortcut-learning experiment (Tab. 2) is well designed, using the confounded vs. clean split protocol of CLEVR-Hans and reporting a validation-test gap metric; NCV shows measurably better robustness with modest amounts of clean data.

Unusually honest treatment of limitations: Suppl. A.5 explicitly acknowledges that the mutual-information guarantees do not quantitatively transfer to the high-dimensional multi-class concept setting, that soundness is only against the trained adversary class, and the Discussion admits accuracy degradation on ImageNet-1k and dependence on concept-extractor quality.
Detailed reproducibility information: architectures, hyperparameters, seeds, and training times are documented across Suppl. C-F.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the core contribution is instantiating the existing Merlin-Arthur classifier on top of off-the-shelf concept extractors (NCB, SpLiCE/CLIP) with a frozen extractor and nonlinear verifier; no new theoretical results are proven, and the 'verifiable' framing is qualified heavily in the supplement (guarantees are heuristic, soundness is only w.r.t. the trained Morgana, one-vs-rest reduction only).

Evaluation of the interpretability claims is largely qualitative. The central selling point — human-understandable concept explanations (Figs. 3-4) — lacks any human study or quantitative interpretability/faithfulness metric beyond completeness/soundness, and for CLIP-derived concepts (LAION caption phrases) the semantic quality of 'concepts' like 'cappuchino' is not validated.

Near-perfect soundness (99.9-100%) paired with substantially lower completeness raises questions about heavy use of the rejection class ⊥; the rejection/abstention rate is never reported, making it hard to interpret what the soundness numbers actually certify.

Some baseline comparisons appear asymmetric: Pixel-MAC uses a ResNet-18 verifier (even on CIFAR-100/ImageNet where the black-box baseline is ResNet-50) and collapses on CIFAR-100 (15.27%), suggesting a training-failure baseline rather than a fair PVG comparison; the SpLiCE-based CBM baseline also omits the per-sample optimization step.

The concept extractor is frozen, so all verifiability guarantees are conditional on a fixed representation whose own biases, leakage, and shortcut structure are outside the game — this somewhat weakens the 'verifiable AI' narrative, as the prover-verifier guarantees cannot detect concept-level artifacts.

Trade-offs are not fully explored: the improvement over the nonlinear CBM baseline (same concept space, non-interpretable head) is small on CLEVR-Hans3/7 and ImageNet-1k and negative on ImageNet, so the significance of the PVG machinery beyond the adversarial-prover regularization effect (which the γ ablation shows drives soundness) remains somewhat unclear.

strengths: The core idea of moving the prover–verifier interaction from pixel space to a compact, interpretable concept space is sensible and addresses a genuine scalability limitation of Merlin–Arthur classifiers (Wäldchen et al., 2024), with Figure 1/2 clearly motivating the work.

The evaluation is broad: five datasets spanning synthetic (CLEVR-Hans) and real-world (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, COCOLogic) data, 10–20 random seeds, ablations over mask size, verifier/prover architecture, and the γ trade-off (Suppl. E.4 shows soundness collapses without the adversarial prover), plus computational cost reporting (Suppl. F).

The supplementary is unusually candid: Suppl. A.5 explicitly states that the information-theoretic guarantees are an 'idealised theoretical lens' rather than quantitative certificates, and the Discussion honestly notes dependence on concept-extractor quality, training instability, and inherited CLIP biases.
The shortcut-learning study (Tab. 2) is a useful diagnostic design, tracking validation–test gaps across varying ratios of clean data.
weaknesses: The soundness metric is much weaker than the framing suggests. Near-perfect soundness (99.99–100.00) is computed only against a single trained Morgana with symmetric architecture and a constrained search procedure — the paper itself concedes (Suppl. A.5) this is robustness 'against this trained adversary class, not an arbitrary worst-case adversary.' Since soundness also counts abstentions (∈ {y, ⊥}), a verifier that abstains on adversarial subsets can trivially inflate soundness; the paper never reports the abstention rate, so the headline 'perfect soundness' claims are hard to interpret.

The central 'verifiability' contribution is thin. No new theory is provided — the paper instantiates existing MAC results under assumptions (bounded AFC κ, relative success rate α, class imbalance B) that are never estimated or verified, and admits (Suppl. A.5) that average precision / MI bounds are not even numerically estimable in their regime. The practical guarantees thus reduce to standard accuracy plus a heuristic adversarial-training regularizer, which weakens the abstract's claim of 'formal verifiability.'

Accuracy gains over concept-extractor-only baselines are modest and inconsistent. On CLEVR-Hans3, NCB pretraining alone already achieves 98.13 test accuracy (Tab. 5); NCV reaches 98.92. On ImageNet-1k, NCV (67.04) is clearly worse than ResNet-50 (76.01) and slightly worse than a nonlinear CBM (69.02), yet the abstract claims NCV 'outperforms' the relevant baselines. The comparison against Pixel-MAC is also uninformative where Pixel-MAC essentially fails (15–42% accuracy), making the 'scales PVGs' claim somewhat built-in by construction of the baseline.

Interpretability claims rest entirely on qualitative examples (Figs. 3–4) with no human evaluation or quantitative concept-quality metrics, despite human-understandability being a core motivation (Fig. 1(ii)). CLIP/SpLiCE-derived concepts are known to be noisy, and the paper cites work (Debole et al., 2025) showing such concept spaces diverge from expert semantics — undermining the explanation-quality claims.

The shortcut-mitigation claim is overstated. In the hardest setting (0% clean data), NCV's validation–test gap (5.23 / 6.15) is worse than the linear CBM (5.11 / 5.10) on CLEVR-Hans3 and comparable on CLEVR-Hans7; benefits only emerge when clean data is added, at which point all models improve. This is a narrower result than 'NCV helps mitigate shortcut behavior.'

The method is an assembly of existing components (MAC game, NCB/SpLiCE extractors, Set Transformers/MLPs) with a heuristic training procedure (soft masks for gradient flow, hard top-m discretization for Arthur, two-phase min–max updates) that has no convergence or stability analysis — a notable omission given the authors themselves flag min–max instability as a known challenge.

Several baselines and the primary concept extractor (NCB), plus one of the main benchmarks (COCOLogic), originate from the authors' own group, raising the question of whether the chosen comparisons are the most independent or competitive ones available (e.g., other nonlinear concept classifiers or abstinence-based interpretable models are largely absent).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated combination of two research lines: the paper identifies a genuine scalability bottleneck of Merlin-Arthur Classifiers (pixel-space explanations) and an expressivity bottleneck of linear CBMs, and proposes a sensible unification that operates the prover-verifier game in concept space.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five datasets spanning synthetic (CLEVR-Hans3/7) and real-world (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, COCOLogic) settings, 10-20 random seeds per setting, ablations over mask size, feature-selector architecture, and the weighting parameter gamma, plus a DCR comparison and wall-clock cost analysis (Table 11).

Honest treatment of the theory: Supplement A.1-A.5 carefully instantiates the Merlin-Arthur guarantees for concept space and explicitly states that the information-theoretic bounds are an 'idealised lens' rather than finite-sample certificates, including a candid discussion of why average precision/MI lower bounds cannot be reliably estimated in high-dimensional sparse concept spaces.

Interesting empirical findings: NCV matches or exceeds strong black-box ResNet baselines on several benchmarks while providing sparse concept-based explanations, and the shortcut-learning study (Table 2) with controlled clean-data ratios is a well-designed experiment showing reduced validation-test gaps.

The gamma sweep (Fig. 5) convincingly demonstrates that the adversarial prover is necessary for soundness (collapsing to 10-52% at gamma=0) while completeness is preserved, supporting the design choice.
Thorough supplementary material with implementation details for all baselines, enabling reproduction of the experimental setup.
weaknesses: The central 'verifiability' framing is stronger than what is actually delivered. Soundness is measured only against the trained Morgana (a specific neural adversary with symmetric architecture), not a worst-case adversary, and the paper itself concedes that the theoretical guarantees are not empirically calibrated. Main-text claims such as 'provably rely on sparse subsets' and 'certifiable decision-making' risk overstating the guarantees relative to Suppl. A.5.

The mechanism behind the accuracy gains is confounded: NCV's completeness largely matches the nonlinear CBM baseline on the same concept encodings (e.g., CLEVR-Hans3: 98.13 vs 98.92; ImageNet-1k: NCV 67.04 is actually below nonlinear CBM 69.02). Since Merlin-only training (gamma=0) already retains high completeness, the headline accuracy improvements appear attributable to sparse nonlinear concept classification rather than the prover-verifier game per se. An ablation isolating the game's contribution to accuracy (e.g., a sparse top-k nonlinear classifier without provers) is missing.

Near-perfect soundness (99.9-100%) across all datasets raises the concern that the concept-space game is trivially easy and Morgana is weak, which would undermine the robustness interpretation (the theory requires a non-degenerate relative success rate alpha, which the paper admits it does not estimate).

The quality of explanations rests heavily on the underlying concept extractor (NCB, CLIP-Sim), and interpretability is assessed only qualitatively (Figs. 3-4); no human evaluation or quantitative faithfulness metric beyond completeness/soundness is provided. The 'mugs and cups and extend and support and cappuchino' style explanations in Fig. 3 illustrate that concept quality may be limited in practice.
The Pixel-MAC baseline appears possibly under-tuned (15.27% on CIFAR-100 with a 32-pixel mask), which strengthens NCV's relative advantage; a more careful discussion of baseline tuning would help.

No explicit code release is mentioned, and some key quantities (mask sizes, gamma) were presumably selected using validation sets, but the selection protocol is not always explicit; given the multi-component min-max training, full reproducibility without code is uncertain.
No formal discussion of research ethics beyond inherited CLIP/LAION dataset biases (acknowledged but briefly).
